gela-002.title: The magnetic flip that starts the Quaternary
gela-002.text: About 2.58 Ma, Earth's magnetic field flipped. It went from normal polarity, the Gauss Chron, to reversed polarity, the Matuyama Chron. Geologists use the flip as a marker. It defines the base of the Gelasian, and so the start of both the Pleistocene and the Quaternary, with the reference section at Monte San Nicola in Sicily. In 2009 the boundary was moved down to 2.58 Ma to match key changes in climate, oceans and life at that time. The flip coincides with a minor extinction of calcareous nannofossils, tiny chalky plankton, among them Discoaster pentaradiatus and Discoaster surculus. The weakened field may have left Earth's surface unshielded for about 15,000 years from the radiation of a supernova.

gela-004.title: The Quaternary ice age begins
gela-004.text: At the height of the glacials, ice at least 4 km thick covered parts of Europe, North America and Siberia. That world began around 2.58 Ma, when ice sheets started to spread across the Northern Hemisphere. This was the start of the Quaternary glaciation, and it is still going on. The start of the Quaternary is tied to the formation of the Arctic ice cap. Greenland had been icing over since the late Pliocene, as {{ref:plio-058}} describes. From then on, glacials and interglacials, cold spells and warmer breaks, alternated. Through the Pleistocene, mean temperatures fell and the swings between the two grew larger. The south felt it too. In the first Pleistocene glacial, Patagonian ice reached the present Argentine coast.

gela-003.title: Mastodons and gomphotheres vanish outside the Americas
gela-003.text: The elephant's relatives had once roamed widely across the Old World. During the Early Pleistocene, every proboscidean outside the Americas that was not a true elephant died out. Mammutids, gomphotheres and deinotheres all disappeared. Only Stegodon survived. Outside the Americas, the trunked mammals were reduced to the elephant family and that one holdout. It was a sharp narrowing for a group that had spread out of Africa in {{ref:mioc-037}}.

gela-005.title: The Eltanin asteroid strikes the deep ocean
gela-005.text: An asteroid about 1–4 km wide plunged into the deep ocean at the edge of the Bellingshausen Sea, about 1,500 km southwest of Chile. It hit sea floor 4–5 km deep and left no known crater. Scientists found the site from an iridium anomaly, an excess of a metal rare on Earth but common in asteroids, in sediment cores. The impact probably vaporized about 150 km³ of water. It raised tsunami waves hundreds of metres high.

gela-006.title: Ice at both poles dries the planet
gela-006.text: With ice now at both poles, the globe dried out. That drying sped up a long decline in the functional diversity of hoofed mammals around 2.5 Ma, the range of different ways they made a living. Africa cooled and dried about 2.5 Ma, at the same time as the rise of thick-molared Homo rudolfensis and Paranthropus. In Australia an aridification event at 2.56 Ma may be linked to the start of Arctic glaciation. Around 2.5 Ma, the Omo–Turkana Basin held a mix of forest, woodland, grassland and bushland, and its grasslands kept spreading through the Early Pleistocene.

gela-007.title: Early Homo and robust australopithecines branch out
gela-007.text: About 2.5 Ma, the hominin fossil record of East Africa suddenly fills with variety. Robust australopithecines and early Homo appear first in the Turkana Basin. This looks like an adaptive radiation, a burst of new species filling different ways of life, and it straddles the Pliocene–Pleistocene boundary. The first Homo species appeared about 2.5 Ma. Until then, hominins had kept their tree-climbing habits. Brain size rose quickly, and by 2 Ma the first animals classed in the genus Homo had appeared. For a time, several kinds shared the land. Paranthropus and early Homo coexisted at the start of the Pleistocene. But only Homo erectus remained for much of it, as {{ref:gela-024}} tells.

gela-009.title: Ethiopian waters join the Nile
gela-009.text: About 2.5 Ma, waters from Ethiopia flowed north for the first time and joined the ancestral Egyptian Nile. Farther south, the Rwenzori Mountains rose. Their uplift turned the drainage of paleolake Obweruka east and began forming Lake Victoria, which did not yet drain north.

gela-013.title: Smilodon and the short-faced bear appear
gela-013.text: About 2.5 Ma, the earliest species of the saber-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus evolved. That first Smilodon, S. gracilis, probably descended from Megantereon. It lived until 500,000 years ago and reached northern South America in the Great American Interchange. Smilodon lasted in the Americas until at latest 8,200 years ago, perhaps the last saber-toothed cat.

gela-011.title: Paranthropus boisei shares Africa with early Homo
gela-011.text: Paranthropus boisei, a robust australopithecine, lived in East Africa about 2.5 to 1.15 million years ago. Its oldest remains, from Malema, are about 2.3 million years old. It turns up at Koobi Fora and Olduvai Gorge and outlasted H. habilis. The 1.7-million-year-old skull KNM-ER 406, with a 510 cc brain, shows several hominin species shared Africa at once.

gela-010.title: Lake Bungunnia dams the Murray
gela-010.text: About 2.5 Ma, the Grampians of Victoria rose more than 250 m. Earth movements then blocked the Murray River near Swan Reach. Behind the blockage grew Lake Bungunnia, a vast freshwater lake that lasted from 2.5 to 0.5 Ma.

gela-012.title: Pre-Illinoian ice reaches Kansas and Missouri
gela-012.text: Researchers once counted two great glaciations in North America's early ice age. They now count 11. From about 2.5 to 0.2 million years ago, the continent went through repeated Pre-Illinoian glacial and interglacial periods. The old named stages, the Nebraskan, Aftonian, Kansan and Yarmouthian, were discarded. The Laurentide Ice Sheet reached as far south as the Missouri and Ohio river valleys, and to Douglas County, Kansas. Later Illinoian ice sheets pushed farther still, to near Carbondale, Illinois. Patchy glacial drift, debris dumped by the ice, more than 500,000 years old survives in parts of the Driftless Area of the upper Mississippi.

gela-014.title: The last seaway across Panama closes
gela-014.text: The seaway between the Americas closed in stages. A collision began about 25 Ma, and deep-ocean connections closed between 12 and 9.2 Ma. Surface water that kept Atlantic and Pacific salinities alike stopped flowing about 4.6 Ma. A last shallow, temporary breach came as recently as 2.45 Ma, and after that the two oceans were sealed apart.

gela-015.title: The Amazon settles into its present course
gela-015.text: The Amazon had already been a transcontinental river since 11.8–11.3 Ma, as {{ref:mioc-099}} describes. It took its present shape later, about 2.4 million years ago. So the river that crosses the continent is old, but its present layout is young. Its shape settled in the same cold, dry stretch that saw ice spread across the north.

gela-017.title: Wind-blown dust builds the Loess Plateau
gela-017.text: About 2.4 Ma, crustal movement and a cold climate started laying down loess on China's Loess Plateau. Loess is fine, wind-blown silt that piles up in thick blankets. Several causes lined up. Tibetan uplift had set up the East Asian monsoon, as {{ref:mioc-007}} describes. Then the drier Quaternary climate weathered out the silt. The winds carried it away and dropped it, layer upon layer, over the plateau.

gela-019.title: Sundaland emerges and mammals reach Java
gela-019.text: Before about 2.4 Ma, Java had no mammals. Then Sundaland, the shallow shelf of Southeast Asia, emerged as sea level fell. Animals walked across from mainland Asia, among them Sinomastodon bumiajuensis, a dwarf elephant relative, and colonized the newly exposed land.

gela-018.title: Oldowan tools spread across and out of Africa
gela-018.text: Between 2.4 and 1.7 million years ago, Oldowan stone tools flourished in eastern Africa and spread to southern Africa. Securely dated Oldowan artifacts 2.4–1.9 million years old at Ain Boucherit, Algeria, carry the industry into North Africa. At Swartkrans, South Africa, Oldowan tools of 2.2–1.8 Ma lie with Paranthropus robustus fossils, and a polished bone point there dates to 1.8–1.5 Ma. The toolmakers also left Africa. By 1.8 Ma early Homo with Oldowan tools lived at Dmanisi, Georgia. The old toolkit proved hard to retire. Even after Acheulean tools appeared about 1.7 Ma, Oldowan tools went on being made, and other traditions replaced them only by about 0.25 Ma.

gela-016.title: Homo habilis, the 'handy man'
gela-016.text: Homo habilis, the 'handy man', lived in East and South Africa from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago. Its brain ranged from about 500 to 900 cm³, and it may still have climbed trees like the australopithecines. It made Oldowan stone tools. Unlike australopithecines, it ate much meat, probably scavenged. Around 2 Ma it may have built the first structures, stones propping up branches. A 1.75 Ma stone circle at Olduvai is the oldest claimed architecture. Whether it was the direct ancestor of Homo erectus is now debated.

gela-020.title: Giant ground sloths walk into North America
gela-020.text: Eremotherium eomigrans, the first megatheriid ground sloth in North America, arrived 2.2 Ma across the new Panamanian land bridge. Traffic ran the other way too. Horses that had entered South America in the Great American Interchange evolved into Hippidion around 2.5 Ma.

gela-021.title: Shangchen: stone tools in China before Dmanisi?
gela-021.text: Possible stone tools at Shangchen in central China are dated to 2.12 Ma, about 300,000 years before Dmanisi. If confirmed, they are the oldest known stone tools outside Africa. They are not alone. Pebble tools are reported from Yiron, Israel, at 2.4 Ma, Riwat, Pakistan, at 2.0 Ma and Renzidong, China, at over 2 Ma. Tools perhaps 2.48 million years old come from the Zarqa Valley in Jordan. Together they suggest that Homo habilis or an even earlier species may have spread across Asia before H. erectus. None of these claims is yet settled.

gela-022.title: The Waiteariki supereruption
gela-022.text: A single huge eruption in New Zealand's Tauranga Volcanic Centre produced the Waiteariki ignimbrite, about 870 ± 87 km³ of dense rock. It probably came from the Omanawa Caldera, known only from a gravity anomaly. At least eight other large eruptions struck the area between 2.4 and 1.9 million years ago.

gela-023.title: Huckleberry Ridge, Yellowstone's greatest eruption
gela-023.text: The Huckleberry Ridge eruption made about 2,500 times as much ash as Mount St. Helens in 1980. Its ash is found from southern California to St. Louis. Yellowstone volcanism began 2.15 Ma, and its first and largest cycle climaxed in this VEI 8 eruption. It produced about 2,450–2,500 km³ of material and left the Island Park Caldera, roughly 80 by 65 km. Part of the tuff records a brief wobble of Earth's magnetic field, the Huckleberry Ridge excursion, and is dated very precisely to 2.0773 ± 0.0034 Ma.

gela-024.title: Homo erectus appears in Africa
gela-024.text: A 2.04-million-year-old skull from Drimolen in South Africa, DNH 134, is the oldest identified Homo erectus. Its owner lived alongside Paranthropus robustus. Other early fossils include the roughly 1.9-million-year-old KNM-ER 2598 and the cranium KNM-ER 3733 from Koobi Fora, Kenya. H. ergaster, often treated as African H. erectus, was the first human with a slender, modern body plan. Its populations spread through grassland and woodland savannas. Those were expanding as the globe dried at the onset of the Quaternary glaciation. The species proved durable. Most H. erectus fossils date from 1.8 to 1 Ma, and it lasted until about 0.6 Ma. For a long time it was the only hominin, the survivor of the crowded field in {{ref:gela-007}}, and the first to spread out of Africa, as {{ref:gela-028}} tells.

gela-025.title: The Altiplano–Puna eruptions die down
gela-025.text: The giant Andean eruptions did not stop at once. Large ignimbrites kept coming in the central Andes, including the 550 km³ Galán ignimbrite about 2.1 Ma. After 2 Ma, activity in the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex waned. After 1 Ma it was mostly andesitic, a less explosive kind of lava, with no large ignimbrites.

gela-028.title: Homo spreads out of Africa
gela-028.text: The earliest hominins outside Africa date to close to 2 million years ago. They mark the start of expansions led by Homo erectus. In the Early Pleistocene, archaic Homo arose in Africa and spread through Africa and Eurasia, in waves known together as Out of Africa I. The key early sites trace the route. Riwat in Pakistan dates to about 2 Ma, Dmanisi in the Caucasus to 1.81 Ma, and Ubeidiya in the Levant to 1.5 Ma. Climate opened the door. Favorable swings probably opened the Levantine corridor to the adaptable Homo erectus, perhaps only at times. The dispersal has been linked to the Saharan pump around 1.9 Ma, the idea that wet spells greened the Sahara and let animals cross it. By 2.0–1.5 Ma hominins were settling southern Europe and Asia.

gela-029.title: Homo rudolfensis in East Africa
gela-029.text: Homo rudolfensis lived in East Africa about 2 million years ago. Most of its fossils come from Koobi Fora and date to 1.9–1.85 Ma. Its molar enamel was almost as thick as that of Paranthropus. Fossils from Ethiopia and Malawi dated 2.5–2.4 Ma could make it the earliest known Homo, but which specimens belong to it is disputed.

gela-030.title: Kap København: a lost Greenland world in DNA
gela-030.text: Mastodons once lived in northern Greenland. Environmental DNA, genetic traces left in sediment, from the Kap København Formation is at least two million years old. It records mastodons, Arctic hares, geese, poplar, birch and willow, horseshoe crabs and corals. Average minimum temperatures there were more than 10 °C warmer than today.

gela-034.title: South America's native predators fade further
gela-034.text: The saber-toothed thylacosmilids were among South America's only large mammal predators in the Pliocene, and they died out about 2 Ma. Their placental counterparts, dogs, weasels and saber-toothed cats, entered South America only in the early Pleistocene. Bears, cats and skunks arrived by about 1 Ma, when the short-faced bear Arctotherium first appears there. The traffic ran north as well. The terror bird Titanis had crossed into North America, but it died out there about 1.8 Ma, perhaps outcompeted by carnivorans. The collapse that began in {{ref:plio-051}} was now complete.

gela-035.title: The Taupō Rift opens in New Zealand
gela-035.text: About 2 Ma, the Taupō Rift and the old Taupō Volcanic Zone formed in New Zealand. Their birth ended major activity in the Coromandel Volcanic Zone. The postulated Omanawa Caldera sat where the old and new rifts met.

gela-027.title: The Congo basin takes its present shape
gela-027.text: The Congo River had a long history of rearrangement, as the rising rift flanks in {{ref:mioc-034}} show. Between about 2.0 and 1.5 Ma, its basin finally acquired its present shape. The great drainage of central Africa took the outline it still has.

gela-026.title: Ice-age floods deepen the Grand Canyon
gela-026.text: From about 2 Ma, wetter ice-age climates swelled the Colorado River, and it cut the Grand Canyon faster than ever before. By 1.2 million years ago the canyon had almost reached its modern depth. Nearby, the upper half of Zion Canyon was carved between about 2 and 1 million years ago.

gela-036.title: Australopithecus sediba at Malapa
gela-036.text: In Malapa Cave, South Africa, lay two partial skeletons, a juvenile and an adult female, about 1.98 million years old. They belong to Australopithecus sediba, which lived alongside Paranthropus robustus and Homo erectus. Malapa may have been a natural death trap. Once proposed as an ancestor of Homo, it may instead be a late relative of A. africanus; the question is contested.

gela-037.title: The Acheulean: a toolkit for a million years
gela-037.text: Acheulean technology first developed about 2 million years ago, growing out of the Oldowan. Finds from Ethiopia date to 1.95 Ma, and Homo erectus is credited with inventing it, refining the older toolkit it had inherited. Early Acheulean tools from West Turkana, Kenya, date to about 1.76 Ma, and those at Kokiselei to 1.7–1.6 Ma. It traveled. Between 1.5 Ma and about 800,000 years ago, it spread from Africa to Asia, the Middle East and Europe, reaching southern India by 1.51 Ma. Its end is poorly defined. Counting the Sangoan, it lasted until as late as 130,000 years ago.

openers.quaternary-period: Around 2.58 million years ago, ice sheets began to spread across the Northern Hemisphere, and the Quaternary glaciation began. It is still going on. The start is marked by a flip in Earth's magnetic field, from normal to reversed polarity. In North America, glacials and interglacials began to alternate again and again. In Africa, the hominin family branched out, and early Homo appeared beside robust australopithecines.
openers.pleistocene-epoch: The Pleistocene is the age of ice, and it began about 2.58 million years ago as ice sheets spread across the Northern Hemisphere. Ice at both poles dried the globe. Old groups lost ground: outside the Americas, every trunked mammal except the elephants and Stegodon died out. New hunters arrived, among them the saber-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus. In East Africa, hominin fossils became extraordinarily diverse.
openers.gelasian-age: The Gelasian, the first age of the Pleistocene, opens with Earth's magnetic field flipping about 2.58 million years ago. Ice sheets spread across the north, and the last shallow sea link across Panama closed no later than 2.45 million years ago. An asteroid hit the deep ocean southwest of Chile. Rivers and lakes rearranged too: Ethiopian waters joined the Nile, and earth movements dammed the Murray River into vast Lake Bungunnia. In East Africa, robust australopithecines such as Paranthropus boisei lived beside early Homo.

reviews.gelasian-age: Ice set the terms of the Gelasian. Ice at both poles dried the globe, grasslands spread, and loess piled up on China's plateau. In that drier Africa, hominins branched out, from Paranthropus with its heavy molars to Homo habilis, Homo erectus and the Oldowan and Acheulean toolkits. With the Americas now joined, South America's native predators faded and northern animals poured in. And Homo erectus walked out of Africa, reaching Dmanisi and settling southern Europe and Asia.
